name: Pimecrolimus

card.summary: A prescription calcineurin-inhibitor cream (Elidel) used on eczema, including on the face and eyelids, where it calms redness and scaling without the skin thinning linked to long-term steroid creams.
card.note: US label carries a boxed warning about a possible cancer risk; prescription only.

quick.overview:
Pimecrolimus is a non-steroid cream prescribed for atopic dermatitis (eczema). People care about it for appearance because inflamed, flaky or red facial and eyelid skin is visible, and because it is an alternative to topical steroids, which can thin facial skin with prolonged use.

It works by blocking calcineurin in T-cells, which lowers the inflammatory signals behind the rash. A large network meta-analysis found it improved most outcomes studied in eczema, and a five-year trial in infants compared it with steroid creams.
quick.how: It is applied as a 1% cream to affected skin on a dermatologist's or physician's prescription, usually for flares and often on sensitive areas such as the face, eyelids and skin folds. Clinicians also use it off-label for conditions such as seborrheic dermatitis, vitiligo and some other inflammatory skin conditions.
quick.risks: Common effects include burning or warmth where applied. In 2006 the US FDA added a boxed warning about a possible risk of skin cancer and lymphoma; dermatology and allergy societies objected that causation had not been shown, and a 2023 meta-analysis reported no increased cancer risk.

lead: Pimecrolimus is a topical calcineurin inhibitor developed by Novartis and sold as Elidel. The FDA approved it on 13 December 2001 for atopic dermatitis.[1]

For appearance, its value is on visible skin: eczema on the face and eyelids produces redness, dryness and scaling, and pimecrolimus can be used there without the skin atrophy associated with prolonged topical corticosteroids.[1][3] It is therefore a common option for sensitive facial areas.

It binds the protein FKBP1A and inhibits calcineurin, reducing T-cell activation and cytokine release, and it also limits mediator release from mast cells.[1] Dermatology guidance lists it with tacrolimus as a first-line topical option that can be used alongside topical steroids.[3]

chain: Calmer, more even skin on face and eyelids
angle.text: Pimecrolimus treats the inflammatory condition causing visible redness and flaking, particularly on thin facial skin where steroid creams are used cautiously. The visible change is an outcome of treating the underlying dermatitis.

paras: Pimecrolimus is approved for atopic dermatitis and is described as an option when corticosteroids and moisturisers are insufficient.[1][3] Reports and trials also cover seborrheic dermatitis, cutaneous lupus, oral lichen planus, vitiligo and psoriasis, which are off-label.[1][4][5][6]
Because it does not thin skin the way topical steroids can, it is used on the face, eyelids and folds.[1]

A 2023 systematic review and network meta-analysis of 219 trials in 43,123 patients reported high-certainty evidence that pimecrolimus improved six of seven eczema outcomes, among the best for two.[2] A five-year randomised trial in 2,418 infants found more than 85% overall and 95% facial treatment success in both pimecrolimus and steroid groups, with far fewer steroid days in the pimecrolimus group.[7]

In January 2006 the FDA required a boxed warning about a potential increased risk of lymphoma and skin cancer, similar to the tacrolimus warning. The American Academy of Dermatology and the American Academy of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology objected that causation had not been shown, and a 2023 Lancet Child & Adolescent Health meta-analysis found no increased cancer risk with moderate certainty.[1] The five-year infant trial reported adverse-event profiles similar between pimecrolimus and steroid groups.[7]

Pimecrolimus is an ascomycin-derived macrolactam. Compared with tacrolimus it is described as more selective, with less skin penetration and no effect on Langerhans cells.[1] A one-year study measured low blood concentrations in adults using the cream intermittently.[8]

Trials include the network meta-analysis and five-year infant study above,[2][7] an open study in vitiligo,[9] and a trial in cutaneous lupus.[10] Pimecrolimus is also mentioned in reviews of oral lichen planus, lichen sclerosus and psoriasis therapy.[4][5][6]

timeline.event: Meta-analysis in Lancet Child & Adolescent Health reports no increased cancer risk.[1]
